newsitem.title: HAITI: Anti-government strike rocks Haitian capital.
newsitem.headline: Anti-government strike rocks Haitian capital.

text.p: Demonstrators threw rocks and burned tires in an anti-government general strike on Thursday, bringing Haiti's capital to a virtual halt.

The action was called by several popular organisations to protest tough tactics used by the National Police to break up a peaceful demonstration last week, and to call for the resignation of Prime Minister Rosny Smarth.
In that demonstration on Friday, one man's hand was blown off and many people were trampled after police used explosive tear gas canisters to disperse the crowd.

Strike leaders claimed they were supported by members of more than 160 popular organisations. Independent Radio Metropole reported that the strike was observed countrywide, although without the violence found in Port-au-Prince.
"Anyone who wants to go to work because they need money should think about how much it costs to buy a new windscreen," one strike supporter said.
Gangs of young men threw rocks at cars in the working class Carrefour-Feuilles section of Port-au-Prince before police broke up the crowd and made some arrests, witnesses said.

Police fired shots in Cite Soleil slum to disperse crowds who were burning tires. Crowds threatened journalists and passers-by who looked prosperous, using the term "big eater," an epithet used by the poor to describe the rich.
The strike was the latest sign of growing desperation in a country where unemployment is as high as 80 percent and the average yearly income is $250, the lowest in the hemisphere.

President Rene Preval will have held office for one year from next month, but many Haitians say they are frustrated with his government's failure to effect any improvements in the impoverished nation.
The focus of their anger has been the prime minister, an unpopular Preval appointee whom demonstrators said they considered incompetent and called one of the "big eaters."

The Haitian National Police and U.N. peacekeeping troops patroling Haiti promised to guarantee security. Police circled the city and used loudspeakers to offer free rides in the back of their trucks to people stranded by the strike.
Transportation unions had said on Tuesday they would not support the strike but many taxi and bus drivers stayed home on Thursday, leaving residents stranded.

U.N. officials attributed the many closed businesses to intimidation, rather than popular support for the strike. "It is obvious that the majority of those who have stayed home are doing so not because they support the strike but rather to avoid any incident," U.N. spokesman Eric Falt said.
